newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE-Air pollution grips Bangladesh capital.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Air pollution grips Bangladesh capital.

text.p: While tackling maddening evening traffic in one of Dhaka's busiest avenues, police constable Abdus Salam tied a mask around his nose.

"I (have been) using this (mask) for the last three months. Every day, I can't inhale poison for hours," Salam said, adding that air in the Bangladesh capital could be among the most polluted in the world.
The policeman said he had recently suffered chronic headaches, a condition he never had before. And Salam is not alone.
Thousands of residents in the Bangladesh capital, from schoolchildren and office workers to bus drivers, now wear masks when they leave their homes.

"Air pollution in this city of nine million people has really reached an alarming level. It's one of the world's worst, and has crossed all safety limits," Saiyid Mosharraf Husain, Director-General of the Department of Environment (DOE), told Reuters.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has set the maximum acceptable limit of the presence of Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM) at 200 micrograms per cubic metre of air.
In Dhaka, SPM was recently found to be as high as 1,800 micrograms.
MOTOR VEHICLES TO BEAR THE BLAME
While most of the world's pollution-hit cities blame industries, Husain and other experts said motor vehicles were the major polluters in Dhaka.
"They (motors) are 80 percent responsible for this hazard. Most are not fit, use leaded fuel and emit black smoke containing toxic carbon monoxide," said Husain.
Vehicles in Bangladesh use leaded fuel as the country's lone refinery is not technically able to produce lead-free fuel.

"Lead pollution in Dhaka's air is probably the highest among polluted cities, especially during low-rain months," said Dr M. Kholiquzzaman, Chief Scientific Officer of the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission (BAEC).
The BAEC has recently detected, in a survey, 463 nanograms (a billionth of a gram) of lead per cubic metre of air in Dhaka during the months of November to January.
This compares with 360 naograms in Bombay and 383 nanograms in Mexico City.
Old, unfit vehicles and the increasing presence of three-wheelers with two-stroke engines on the Dhaka roads are at the root of the city's carbon monoxide pollution.

One environment official said the majority of the 160,000 motor vehicles in the city had major problems, but obtain certificates easily through the country's weak and corruption-prone checking systems for motor vehicle fitness.
Two-stroke engined vehicles which number about 50,000 in the Dhaka metropolitan area are major pollutants.
"These vehicles are the major culprit. They can't burn fuel fully and thus heavily emit toxic substances," said the DOE chief.
"I am lobbying for a total ban of this transport. India which produces and exports this vehicle is itself phasing them out," he said.
WORRIED RESIDENTS LOOK FOR RELIEF
Deteriorating air quality is a major concern of residents and doctors have warned it is silently and slowly choking thousands of people to death.
A recent survey by a local magazine found increased cases of diseases like asthma, eye infections, kidney failure and respiratory problems in the city's hospitals which doctors linked to toxic air.
"Sometimes I feel like (I'm) living in a gas chamber. I feel so bad when I think my kid is inhaling poison every second and I can't do anything," said Nilufa Begum, 35, a banker.
Doctors warned children are most vulnerable to lead pollution.
"Lead can cause severe intellectual impairment to the children...lead weakens the red blood cells," said physician Professor Abdul Wadud Khan.
LACK OF ACTION ADDS TO THE HAZARD
While experts and citizens are worried about Dhaka's polluted air, the government appears unfazed, according to some environmentalists.

"There is (the) least coordination among different government agencies on pollution control. Everybody reacts so casually when it comes to the issue of environment," said a spokesman of the Bangladesh Environment Lawyers' Association.
The DOE's Husain said he was searching for devices like "magnetizers" which could reduce smoke emissions if fitted in vehicles.
"I am insisting the energy ministry add to the refinery the technology to produce lead-free fuel. I am requesting government offices to convert their vehicles into gas-run," he added.
"But environment (concern) is relatively new thinking in Bangladesh and it will take some more time to expect a concerted action," Husain said.
